p: The phrase the Silk Road will be coined two years hence, in eighteen seventy-seven, by a German geographer named Baron Ferdinand von Richthofen; the pages from the future tell me so, and one of the hazards of my peculiar situation is that I sometimes forget which side of the present I am standing on. The Baron, at any rate, needed a name for the network of routes by which, for some fifteen hundred years, goods and ideas passed overland between China and the Mediterranean, and he chose well, for silk was the most famous of those goods, and the most mysterious.

The Romans knew silk as a precious fabric that came from a land at the end of the world, inhabited by a people they called the Seres, meaning the silk people. They had no idea how it was made; the poet Virgil supposed that it was combed from the leaves of trees. The Chinese had in fact been making it for thousands of years, from the cocoons of a caterpillar fed upon mulberry leaves, and guarded the secret jealously. Roman moralists complained that silk was so fine as to be indecent, and that the fashion for it drained the empire of gold. The elder Pliny, who died in the eruption of Vesuvius, reckoned that India, China and Arabia took a hundred million sesterces a year from the Roman empire. Complaints about the balance of trade with the East are thus very ancient indeed, and the moralists' remedy, that the Romans should simply stop wanting things, was as successful then as it has been since.

The Chinese side of the story begins in about one hundred and thirty-eight years before Christ, when the Han emperor Wu sent an envoy named Zhang Qian westward to seek allies against the nomadic Xiongnu, who troubled China's northern frontier. Zhang Qian was captured by the Xiongnu and held for ten years, during which he married and had a son; he escaped, completed his mission, failed to find his allies, was captured again, escaped again, and returned to China after thirteen years with reports of kingdoms in Central Asia and their marvellous horses. The emperor, who greatly desired the horses, opened the western routes, and the trade began in earnest.

There was never a single road, nor did merchants travel the whole way. Goods passed from hand to hand, through oasis towns on the edges of the terrible deserts of Central Asia, like Kashgar, Samarkand and Bukhara, and over the mountain passes of the Pamirs, a few hundred miles at a time, each merchant selling to the next. Camels, especially the two-humped Bactrian camel which endures the cold, were the ships of these routes. And much of the trade went not overland at all but by sea, from China and India through the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, borne on the monsoon winds, which blow from the south-west in summer and the north-east in winter, so that a ship could sail to India in one season and home in the next.

Silk travelled west, along with porcelain, paper, lacquer and tea. Westward too came Indian spices, cotton and precious stones. East went horses, glass, silver, wool and wine. But the most important cargoes were invisible.

Along these routes, Buddhism travelled from India into Central Asia and China, carried by monks and merchants, and transformed Chinese civilisation; the cave temples of Dunhuang, at the western edge of China, filled with paintings and manuscripts, bear witness to it. Later, Christianity of the Nestorian church reached China under the Tang dynasty, Manichaeism reached it and flourished for a time, and Islam spread across Central Asia. Papermaking passed westward, the tradition says, after a battle at the river Talas in seven hundred and fifty-one, when Chinese prisoners taught the craft to the Arabs of Samarkand; whether the story is exact, paper certainly came west by these routes, and without it the learning of the Islamic world and later the printing of Europe would have been impossible. Arithmetic, astronomy, medicine, music and the arts of the table passed both ways. The road was the university of the ancient world.

It carried diseases too. The Black Death of the fourteenth century, which I shall describe in its place, almost certainly travelled from Central Asia to the Black Sea along the trade routes, and from there by ship to Italy and the rest of Europe. Trade binds the world together for good and ill alike.

The routes flourished most when a single great power kept order along them. Under the Han and the Romans they prospered; in the turmoil after both fell, they declined. They revived under the Tang dynasty of China and the early Islamic caliphs, and most of all under the Mongols in the thirteenth century, when, it was said, a maiden carrying a nugget of gold on her head could travel from one end of the empire to the other unmolested. It was in that age that the Venetian Marco Polo travelled to the court of Kublai Khan, and that envoys of the Pope reached Mongolia. When the Mongol empire broke up and the Ming dynasty turned China inward, and above all when the Portuguese found the sea route round Africa to India at the end of the fifteenth century, the old overland roads fell into decay. The desert sand covered the oasis towns and their libraries.

The men of the future, I see, have revived the name. The government of China in the twenty-first century has proposed a great scheme of railways, ports and roads across Asia and beyond, which it calls the Belt and Road. The camels have been replaced by locomotives. The anxieties of the moralists about the balance of trade, I imagine, have not.
